_README: Electrochemical workstation troubleshooting — Instrumentation spec §33. EVERY entry offers MULTIPLE possible causes; the health check rejects single-cause entries. Diagnostics are ordered cheapest-and-most-likely first, and several deliberately start with 'is it the instrument, the cell, or the processing?' — the §34 separation used as a diagnostic tool. DRAFT — review before treating as teaching material.

items.summary: The voltammogram is buried in noise or shows regular oscillation superimposed on the response.
causes: Electrical interference picked up on long or poorly routed leads — mains pickup is the usual suspect
Poor or intermittent connection at any of the three electrodes
Control-loop oscillation from a high-impedance or partially blocked reference electrode
Bandwidth or stability setting inappropriate for the cell
Over-applied iR compensation driving the loop unstable
Current range far above the actual signal, so the measurement sits in the noise floor
Inadequate shielding — no Faraday cage where the currents are small
A genuinely unstable cell: bubbling, convection, or an evolving surface
diagnostics: First separate instrument from cell: is the noise periodic at mains frequency (instrument or shielding) or random and irregular (often the cell)?
Check every connection physically before changing any settings — intermittent contact is the most common cause and the quickest to rule out.
Reduce the current range to match the actual signal and repeat.
Set iR compensation to zero and repeat. If the noise disappears, it was over-compensation.
Move the cell into a Faraday cage, or simply shorten and re-route the leads.
Check the reference electrode: a blocked frit raises its impedance and destabilises the loop.
fixes: Shorten and re-route leads; keep them away from mains cabling and stirrer motors
Use a Faraday cage for small currents
Select an appropriate current range
Reduce or remove iR compensation
Replace or refresh the reference electrode
Adjust the bandwidth or stability setting if your instrument exposes one

items.symptom: Unexpectedly large semicircle in the Nyquist plot
items.summary: The impedance arc is much larger than expected, implying a high charge-transfer resistance.
causes: Genuinely slow interfacial kinetics
Poor electrical contact anywhere in the cell, adding resistance that the fit attributes to charge transfer
Incomplete wetting, so the electrochemically active area is far smaller than assumed
An unstable or evolving interface — the spectrum is describing a moving target
Incorrect cell connection, so the measurement is not of the intended interface
An inappropriate equivalent circuit, so a feature that is not a charge-transfer arc is being fitted as one
Measurement made at a DC bias where the kinetics genuinely are slow
diagnostics: Before interpreting anything, validate the spectrum: check the open-circuit potential was stable, and halve the amplitude to confirm linearity.
Check the high-frequency intercept. If the ohmic resistance is also unexpectedly high, the problem is more likely contact or electrolyte than kinetics.
Re-measure after a longer rest — an interface still evolving gives an arc that shrinks or moves between successive spectra.
Re-assemble the cell and repeat. A large change points to contact rather than kinetics.
Measure at a different DC bias: charge-transfer resistance is bias-dependent, so a single spectrum is a single operating point.
Try a simpler circuit. If it fits comparably, the elaborate one was not justified.
fixes: Improve contact and re-assemble
Allow full wetting before measuring
Wait for a stable open-circuit potential before starting the sweep
Report the DC bias with every spectrum
Justify the circuit on physical grounds before fitting, not after

items.summary: The potential will not settle, or keeps sliding in one direction.
causes: Insufficient equilibration time — the cell simply has not finished settling
Incomplete wetting of a porous electrode
Reference electrode problem: drying out, a blocked frit, or a changed filling solution
A genuinely unstable interface, corroding or dissolving
Cell leakage or evaporation of the electrolyte
Temperature drift in the laboratory
Electrical noise picked up on the high-impedance sensing path
diagnostics: Look at the SHAPE, not the endpoint. A drift rate that decreases means slow equilibration; a roughly constant drift rate means something is continuously changing.
Test the reference against a second, known-good reference in the same electrolyte. This is the single most informative check and is often skipped.
Extend the rest substantially and see whether it eventually settles.
Check for leakage, evaporation and bubbles at the electrode surface.
Record the laboratory temperature alongside the potential.
Swap in a fresh cell with the same reference to separate cell from reference.
fixes: Allow longer equilibration, judged by drift rate rather than elapsed time
Refresh, refill or replace the reference electrode
Seal the cell against evaporation
Improve shielding of the sensing leads
Control the laboratory temperature, or at least record it

materialNotes.material.ntp: This record names self-discharge from dissolved oxygen: an aqueous cell can lose charge while doing nothing.
materialNotes.material.ltp: This record names the same dissolved-oxygen self-discharge, and asks for it to be reported.

items.summary: Current appears where none was expected, or is much larger than the process being studied should produce.
causes: Potential window outside the electrolyte's stability range, so decomposition current is being recorded
Side reactions — dissolved oxygen, water in a nominally non-aqueous system, or impurities
Leakage current through a damaged or contaminated cell
Background current from the electrode substrate or current collector
Incorrect connection, so a different interface is being measured than intended
Instrument compliance reached, giving a response that is not what was requested
Capacitive charging current mistaken for faradaic current, particularly at high scan rates
diagnostics: Run a blank: the same cell and electrolyte with a bare substrate. Whatever current remains is background, not your material. This is the most decisive single test.
Narrow the potential window and repeat. Current that disappears was window-related.
Purge the electrolyte and repeat, to test for dissolved oxygen.
Vary the scan rate: capacitive current scales with v, faradaic peaks with v^b. That difference separates them.
Verify the lead connections against the intended configuration.
Check whether compliance was reached at any point during the measurement.
fixes: Restrict the potential window to the electrolyte's stable range
Purge dissolved oxygen where the measurement requires it
Use a clean substrate and record its blank response
Correct the cell connections
Report background-corrected data, and state that the correction was applied
safetyNotes: Large unexpected currents can cause gas evolution and heating. Stop the measurement and inspect the cell rather than letting it continue.

materialNotes.material.zn_metal: This record notes hydrogen evolution competes with plating below about pH 12.9 — current that is not storing charge.
materialNotes.material.pbo2: This record states the electrode sits 0.46 V above the oxygen line, so oxygen evolution runs in parallel with charging and is indistinguishable from it in a simple current measurement.
materialNotes.material.ni_oh2: This record notes charging sits close to the oxygen line at pH 14, so charge efficiency falls at high state of charge — expected behaviour, not a fault.

items.summary: The response shows regular high-frequency oscillation that is not a property of the cell.
causes: High-impedance reference electrode — a blocked frit or a dried-out reference
Over-applied iR compensation
Bandwidth or stability setting too high for the cell
Long leads adding inductance, particularly in the counter-electrode path
A very low-impedance cell driven by an instrument configured for a high-impedance one
diagnostics: Set iR compensation to zero. If the oscillation stops, it was over-compensation — this is the quickest check and a very common cause.
Substitute a known-good reference electrode.
Reduce the bandwidth or stability setting if your instrument exposes one.
Shorten the leads and re-route them.
Recognise the signature: oscillation is regular and at a frequency unrelated to your scan rate, which is what distinguishes it from real electrochemistry.
fixes: Remove or substantially reduce iR compensation
Replace or refresh the reference electrode
Lower the bandwidth setting
Shorten and re-route cabling
safetyNotes: A loop oscillating at large amplitude can drive the cell well outside its intended potential window. Stop the measurement rather than letting it run.
